analysis.time: As of 20 September 2026, the Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease outbreak was ongoing, with 63 of 167 health zones (37.7%) across seven provinces reporting at least one confirmed case, and 55 health zones across five provinces remaining classified as active transmission zones. The report was published on 25 September 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is concentrated in eastern DR Congo, specifically in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé provinces. It affects human populations, with community deaths accounting for the majority of newly reported deaths.

analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has resulted in a significant case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC, with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for 93.4 per cent of all newly reported cases. Community deaths continue to dominate, indicating ongoing challenges in early detection, timely referral, and access to care.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The outbreak is ongoing, with localized progress observed in parts of the response. However, mortality remains a significant concern. The report emphasizes the need to sustain disease surveillance, response, and preparedness capacities in affected provinces and maintain readiness in neighboring countries.

analysis.brief_en: The IOM Situation Report No. 19, dated 25 September 2026, details a multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). As of 20 September 2026, the outbreak had resulted in 7,733 confirmed cases, 3,732 deaths, and 1,902 recoveries, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Transmission is concentrated in eastern DRC, particularly in Ituri, North Kivu, and Haut-Uélé provinces, where 61 new cases were reported, with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for 93.4 per cent of these. The report highlights ongoing challenges in early detection, timely referral, and access to care, especially in areas affected by displacement, insecurity, and population movement. The outbreak remains active, with 55 health zones across five provinces classified as active transmission zones. The IOM emphasizes the need to sustain disease surveillance, response, and preparedness capacities in affected provinces and maintain readiness in neighboring countries connected through cross-border mobility corridors.

The Bundibugyo virus outbreak, primarily affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is one of the largest on record, with cases rising at a worrying pace. No vaccine is currently approved against the virus, so efforts are focused on advancing vaccine candidates into testing. The rVSV platform, used in the licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, is being leveraged to accelerate development. If early phase trials succeed, the vaccine technology will be transferred to a large-scale manufacturer to produce additional doses for later-stage trials. This initiative aims to ensure rapid, affordable supply of the vaccine in outbreak-affected countries and low- and middle-income settings, provided regulatory approval is obtained. The collaboration highlights the importance of cross-sector efforts in addressing global health challenges like Bundibugyo outbreaks.

The outbreak highlights challenges in timely case detection and access to adequate patient care, which can lead to preventable illness and deaths. The risk of cross-border transmission has increased due to the geographic expansion.

title: UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 31 August - ReliefWeb

analysis.time: The report was published on 25 September 2026, with the event date being 31 August 2026. The outbreak continued to expand geographically during August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), specifically in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and Bas-Uélé provinces. Women and girls represent 53% of reported cases, and children under 17 account for approximately 30.2% of cases and 21.8% of reported deaths.
analysis.event: An Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus was reported in the DRC. UNICEF and the Government of the DRC are scaling up their response efforts, including community-based surveillance and support for essential services.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of 31 August 2026, the DRC reported 2,581 confirmed cases and 1,420 deaths from the Bundibugyo virus. Cumulative confirmed cases reached 6,186, with 3,007 deaths, resulting in a case fatality ratio of 48.6%. The outbreak expanded to six provinces, with 42 health workers affected during August 2026.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: UNICEF is supporting Government-led efforts in community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, and ensuring the continuity of essential services. Contact tracing coverage reached 88%, and 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health and nutrition assistance in August 2026. A funding gap of US$79 million remains.

analysis.brief_en: The UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3, dated 31 August 2026, highlights the ongoing Bundibugyo virus outbreak, which has become the largest ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. As of 31 August, the outbreak had resulted in 6,186 confirmed cases and 3,007 deaths, with a case fatality ratio of 48.6%. The outbreak has spread to six provinces, including Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and Bas-Uélé, with Ituri accounting for 81.9% of all cases. Women and girls represent 53% of reported cases, and children under 17 make up 30.2% of cases and 21.8% of deaths, with children under five bearing the greatest burden. During August, 42 health workers were affected, underscoring risks to frontline responders. UNICEF has scaled up its response to 60 affected health zones and trained 11,723 community actors, including 6,546 community mobilizers. Contact tracing coverage reached 88%, and 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health assistance. The report also mentions measures to ensure the safe reopening of schools in affected provinces. UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan, with US$34.4 million mobilized as of 31 August, leaving a US$79 million funding gap.

title: An approved Ebola antibody may miss its mark against Bundibugyo virus

analysis.time: The study was conducted using genomes collected in 2007, 2012, and 2026, with the 2026 outbreak occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. The publication date is 2026-09-28.
analysis.location_and_population: The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. The study analyzed 44 Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) genomes, including 12 from the 2026 outbreak.
analysis.event: A study published in Nature Communications investigated the efficacy of approved and experimental Ebola monoclonal antibodies against the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) during the 2026 outbreak. The research modeled antibody binding behavior against BDBV and found that some approved treatments may not be effective.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study focused on the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak, which involved 12 genomes from the DRC and Uganda. The research highlighted the genetic divergence between BDBV and Ebola virus (EBOV), suggesting that approved EBOV therapeutics may not be effective against BDBV. The findings emphasize the need for experimental testing to determine the efficacy of treatments against BDBV.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study used computational models to predict antibody binding behavior and concluded that further experimental validation is needed. The authors caution that these findings should not be used alone to alter clinical practice, as they cannot capture the dynamic physiological movements of the viral glycoprotein or the full complexity of real-world antibody binding.

analysis.brief_en: A recent study published in Nature Communications investigated the efficacy of approved and experimental Ebola monoclonal antibodies against the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) during the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. Researchers analyzed 44 BDBV genomes, including 12 from the 2026 outbreak, and identified key mutations that may affect antibody binding. The study found that the licensed monoclonal antibody mAb114 (Ebanga) would exhibit displaced binding and reduced affinity for BDBV due to epitope mutations. Inmazeb, a triple-antibody cocktail, showed mixed results, with two components failing to bind their intended sites when used as monotherapies but potentially working together. The experimental cocktail MBP134 was predicted to bind effectively due to targeting conserved epitopes. However, the authors emphasized that these computational findings require validation through experimental testing, as they cannot fully capture the dynamic nature of antibody-virus interactions. The study highlights the importance of tailoring treatments to specific viral strains, especially in the context of the 2026 BDBV outbreak, and underscores the need for further research to guide clinical responses in the DRC and Uganda.

analysis.event: Researchers Face Challenges Controlling Bundibugyo Virus Outbreak.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: BDBV can cause severe hemorrhagic disease. No specific licensed vaccine exists for the treatment or prevention of BDBV. Early supportive care and early detection can improve survival. Before 2026, no validated test existed to diagnose BDBV. However, an international network of laboratories evaluated four candidate PCR tests within two weeks, showing no evidence of cross-reactivity with Zaire ebolavirus.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: An international network of laboratories, including DZIF, NUM, and European research consortia, evaluated four candidate PCR tests within two weeks. The comprehensive assessment showed no evidence of cross-reactivity. A BDBV vaccine is in development.

analysis.brief_en: Researchers in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are facing challenges in controlling the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbreak. The outbreak highlights the difficulties in diagnosing BDBV, as no validated test existed before 2026. Although BDBV is closely related to ebolavirus, standard rapid tests for Zaire ebolavirus do not cross-detect BDBV. analysis.event: The Africa CDC attributed the rapid spread of the Ebola virus in the DRC to delayed detection, diagnostic challenges, insecurity, and mistrust among affected communities. The outbreak involved the Bundibugyo virus, a less commonly detected species, rather than the Zaire strain.

analysis.brief_en: The Africa CDC has identified delayed detection and diagnostic challenges as key factors contributing to the rapid spread of the Ebola virus in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The outbreak, which was officially declared on May 15, 2026, involved the Bundibugyo virus, a less common species, rather than the Zaire strain. Initially, diagnostic kits in the region could not detect the Bundibugyo virus, allowing the disease to spread for months before laboratory confirmation. The outbreak escalated from eight cases in three health zones to over 2,000 cases across 46 health zones, and has since spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces, making it the largest recorded in the DRC. Insecurity and poor access to communities further hindered containment efforts, while community mistrust complicated response activities. The Africa CDC called for increased resources, political support, and community engagement to address these challenges and control the outbreak. They emphasized that security, cooperation, and access to affected areas are equally critical to stopping transmission.

analysis.time: The clinical trial started enrollment and dosing of patients on or about September 23, 2026. The publication date of the news report is September 28, 2026.

analysis.event: NanoViricides announced the initiation of a Phase II clinical trial of NV-387 oral gummies as a treatment for Ebola virus disease. The trial includes four groups: infusion of monoclonal antibody cocktail, infusion of Remdesivir, infusion of both, and a control group with local standard of care. The trial is registered in the Pan African Clinical Trials Registry with the unique identification number PACTR202608748555077.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Approximately 300 patients have been enrolled in the trial across four groups. The trial involves an adaptive, multi-centre approach with a focus on safety and efficacy. analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The trial is currently in the Phase IIA/IIB stage, with enrollment and dosing beginning on September 23, 2026. The trial is registered and has a principal investigator, Patrick de Marie Chimusa Katoto, leading the effort.
